title: Profile a real program
story:
A profiler answers a question a benchmark cannot: not how fast is this function, but where did the time actually go. The answer is regularly somewhere nobody would have proposed, which is the entire reason the tool exists.

There are two families and the difference matters. A sampling profiler interrupts the program many times a second and records what it was doing, producing a statistical picture with very little overhead. An instrumenting profiler records every call, which is exact and slows the program enough to change its behaviour, sometimes enough to move the bottleneck. Sampling is the right default for anything resembling a real workload.

Reading the output has one trap worth naming. Time spent inside a function alone is not the same as time spent inside it and everything it called. A function that appears to consume most of the runtime may be doing nothing but waiting for something further down. Sorting by the first number finds the work; sorting by the second finds the responsible path. Both are needed, and confusing them sends you to optimise a function whose body is three lines long.

beats.broke: Timing whole runs tells you something is slow and nothing about where. Adding timers by hand only measures the places you already suspected, so the measurement confirms the guess it was meant to test.
beats.fix: Profile the whole program and let it report where time was spent. Sampling profilers interrupt periodically and build a statistical picture at low cost; instrumenting profilers record every call for exactness at much higher cost.
beats.cost: Instrumenting changes what it observes, sometimes enough to relocate the bottleneck. Sampling can miss anything short-lived or rare. Both struggle with time spent waiting rather than computing, which is why a program that is mostly idle on network calls can look fast in a CPU profile while being slow to its users.

interview.q: What is the difference between self time and total time in a profile, and when does each mislead?
interview.trap: Using the larger number because it sounds more significant. Total time is larger by construction for anything near the top of the call tree.
interview.answer: Self time is time spent executing that function's own instructions. Total time includes everything it called. Sorting by total time surfaces entry points that are responsible for a lot of work without doing any of it, so optimising them is meaningless. Sorting by self time finds where the work happens but hides the caller that invoked it a thousand times unnecessarily. The usual approach is to find the expensive self time, then walk back up to see who is causing it to be called that often.

blueprint:
total   self   function
          98.2%   0.1%   main()           <- responsible, does nothing
          97.9%   0.3%   process_all()
          96.4%   2.1%   process_one()
          94.0%  94.0%   json.loads()     <- the work is HERE

Optimising main() is meaningless.
Optimising json.loads() is hard.
Asking why process_all() calls it 40,000 times is the win.

CPU profile shows compute. It does not show waiting.
A program 90% blocked on the network looks idle and is slow.
takeaway: Self time finds the work, total time finds who caused it, and a CPU profile is blind to waiting — which is where most web service latency lives.
